run_info.learning_objective_1: Apply the Fourier transform to decompose a time-domain signal into its frequency components and interpret the resulting spectrum.
run_info.learning_objective_2: State the Central Limit Theorem and use it to justify why the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as sample size increases, regardless of population shape.

top_scenario.title: Medical Imaging Analysis for Disease Diagnosis
top_scenario.scenario: A medical research team is developing a system to analyze medical images, such as MRI and CT scans, to diagnose diseases. The system applies the Fourier transform to decompose the images into their frequency components, which helps identify patterns and features indicative of diseases. However, due to the variability of the images, the team needs to repeatedly sample the images to improve the accuracy of the diagnosis. As the sample size increases, the Central Limit Theorem is used to justify why the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality, allowing for more accurate diagnosis.
top_scenario.reason: The medical imaging domain naturally incorporates both learning objectives, and the scenario reveals non-obvious insights into disease diagnosis. Both topics contribute equally to the scenario.

best_question.question: A medical research team is analyzing MRI scans with a sample size of 100 to diagnose diseases. The Fourier transform of the images shows a dominant peak at 25 Hz. If the team increases the sample size to 500, how would the Central Limit Theorem justify the normality of the sampling distribution of the mean, and what implications would this have on the interpretation of the frequency components in relation to disease diagnosis?
best_question.reason: The question requires the student to relate the Central Limit Theorem to the interpretation of frequency components, which involves both learning objectives. However, the question could be improved by making the connection between the two topics more explicit and natural.

thought_process: The question is asking about the effect of increasing the sample size on the normality of the sampling distribution of the mean using the Central Limit Theorem.
The Central Limit Theorem states that the sampling distribution of the mean will be approximately normal if the sample size is large enough.
The question mentions a dominant peak at 25 Hz in the Fourier transform of the images, which suggests that the data is not normally distributed.
I need to relate the Central Limit Theorem to the interpretation of the frequency components in relation to disease diagnosis.
student_attempt.attempt: The Central Limit Theorem states that as the sample size increases, the sampling distribution of the mean will be approximately normal, regardless of the underlying distribution of the data. In this case, increasing the sample size from 100 to 500 will likely make the sampling distribution of the mean more normal. However, the presence of a dominant peak at 25 Hz in the Fourier transform suggests that the data may not be normally distributed. I'm not sure how to directly relate the Central Limit Theorem to the interpretation of the frequency components, but I think that the increased sample size will provide a more accurate estimate of the mean frequency component, which could be useful for disease diagnosis.
student_attempt.conclusion: Increasing the sample size will make the sampling distribution of the mean more normal, which could provide a more accurate estimate of the mean frequency component for disease diagnosis.

solvability.reason: The question provides enough context to understand the problem, and I have enough knowledge of the Central Limit Theorem to attempt a solution.
